deep_why: Bias in language models stems from imbalances in training data where certain groups are misrepresented or stereotyped. The core insight is that a systematic catalogue of test cases across different languages and cultures can expose these imbalances by comparing model outputs to ground-truth fairness standards. By measuring and comparing bias consistently across multilingual settings, researchers can identify where models systematically favor or harm particular groups, revealing which cultural contexts the training data inadequately covered. This systematic mapping across languages and cultures is essential because biases differ: what appears fair in one language or cultural context may perpetuate harm in another, and only side-by-side benchmarking reveals these gaps.

Cross-domain recommendation requires learning what knowledge from one domain actually helps predict choices in another, despite different user populations and item types. The core soundness rests on finding precise alignment between overlapping users or items: using the shared subset as anchors means the model can learn transfer rules without being forced into one rigid pattern. When the method learns independently per scenario using these overlapping guides, it adapts the transfer strategy to fit that particular domain pair rather than imposing a single rule on all scenarios. The dual-stage replay mechanism further protects by fine-tuning which old knowledge to reuse and which to discard, preventing negative transfer where irrelevant knowledge from the source domain actively harms target predictions.

In biomedical knowledge graphs, the absence of an edge does not mean no relationship exists—it often means the relationship is undiscovered or unreported. The core problem is that random negative samples (non-edges treated as false) may actually be true relationships the graph has not yet recorded, corrupting the training signal. By using graph embeddings to select negatives that are unlikely relationships given the learned geometry of the graph, the method avoids mislabeling hidden truths as falsehoods. This targeted selection is mathematically sound because the embedding space clusters semantically similar entities; a negative sampled far from a node in this learned space is genuinely implausible, whereas random sampling risks choosing actually valid but undiscovered relationships.

Federated recommendation must learn item representations that work across devices with radically different user distributions and sparse data, yet the local optimization on each device can drive the item embedding toward a sharp, narrow local solution that works only for that device. Sharpness-aware minimization fixes this by preferring flatter regions of the loss landscape where small perturbations to the embedding do not cause large changes in loss. Flatter regions correspond to embeddings robust across diverse local conditions; sharp minima are brittle, overfitting to a single device's data. By explicitly seeking the flattest loss surface during training, the method ensures the shared item representation generalizes across all devices, preserving alignment and enabling knowledge sharing even when user bases differ drastically.

Efficient crawling of evolving data requires knowing which sources to prioritize based on how often they change and how important that source is to others. The core principle is that an optimal crawling schedule must exploit relationships between sources: if one source frequently updates and many other sources reference it, updating that source first and propagating knowledge of the change through the graph saves redundant re-crawling. A reinforcement learning agent learns to select which source to crawl next by observing state (current graph, update history) and receiving reward based on how fresh information becomes across the whole graph. Over time it discovers that following graph structure beats independent crawling because propagation through relationships multiplies the value of each crawl.

The effectiveness of a chatbot in correcting false beliefs depends on domain context because different domains activate different psychological defenses. Health misinformation triggers trust in personal experience; scientific misinformation triggers disbelief of abstract models; political misinformation triggers identity protection and tribal loyalty. A single chatbot design cannot overcome all these psychological barriers equally because the emotional and cognitive stakes differ across domains. The experiment reveals this by showing the same chatbot works well on health and science but struggles on politics, where identity-protective cognition is strongest. This variation proves that misinformation correction requires domain-aware strategies that address the specific psychological mechanism driving belief in each domain, not one-size-fits-all design.

Multi-hop reasoning in retrieval-augmented systems often loses retrieved evidence mid-chain because each step expands the search tree and earlier evidence gets buried. PruneRAG's core insight is that confidence scores on intermediate answers can guide which branches to continue and which to prune. When an intermediate answer is reliable, there is no need to explore other branches at that step; when it is uncertain, the system should search further. This pruning is sound because it preserves the branches that led to correct answers while cutting wasteful expansions, concentrating retrieval on entity-level details that anchor the chain. The effect is that critical evidence remains activated throughout the reasoning chain instead of being retrieved early but forgotten at branch points.

Heterogeneous graphs have nodes with different amounts of semantic information and relationships that cross node types asymmetrically, making anomaly signals hard to propagate uniformly. The core soundness comes from aligning semantics across types so that anomaly cues flow from rich nodes to sparse nodes without distortion. When multiple task-specific objectives pull the learning in conflicting directions—each node type wants different feature emphasis—adaptive weighting harmonizes these conflicts by letting each task learn without blocking others. This multi-task harmony preserves each type's detection sensitivity while allowing shared features to carry anomaly signals between types. The method works because semantic alignment and task weighting together ensure that informative anomaly patterns from one node type can guide detection in others despite radical differences in node richness.

Immersive educational systems require generating high-quality, personalized content on low-end devices, which is computationally impossible if every interaction runs a full model locally. The core strategy is to retrieve relevant prior knowledge and examples from a store, then let the model focus only on personalization and interaction. This works because retrieval shifts the burden from generating from scratch to selecting and adapting, reducing the model's computational load while still producing contextually grounded responses. Adding digital humans and interactivity creates engagement that makes learning stick, while learning analytics track what each student understands. By distributing work—retrieval handles breadth, local models handle personalization, humans handle engagement—the system delivers rich learning without overloading devices in resource-constrained regions.

Structured data models traditionally trained on single datasets fail to transfer because each dataset has unique columns, distributions, and value ranges. Foundation models for structured data work by pretraining on massive synthetic and real structured data so that the model learns universal patterns—handling missing values, detecting outliers, ranking columns by importance—that apply across any new dataset. In-context learning then adapts this foundational knowledge: showing the model a few examples of the target task teaches it the specific prediction goal without retraining. This is mathematically sound because the pretraining has built a transferable understanding of structured reasoning that in-context examples can steer toward any task, eliminating the need for dataset-specific optimization.

Long-term emotional support requires tracking user state across sessions where new information is implicit, scattered, and contradicted by later disclosures. The core problem is that standard long-context and retrieval systems treat facts as static and explicit, missing the temporal dynamics of evolving emotional states and conflicting information. A robust long-term memory system must extract which facts matter, reason about when they apply (temporal reasoning), detect contradictions across sessions (conflict detection), and know when not to use a fact (abstention). Evaluating these five capabilities separately reveals where systems fail: whether they can ground responses in facts (extraction), track timeline (temporal), or wisely refrain from using outdated information (abstention). This breakdown is essential because emotional support succeeds only when the system remembers not just facts but the human context those facts carry.

Editing images to change emotional tone requires the model to separate emotional content (anger, joy, sadness) from neutral content (objects, people, setting). The core challenge is that emotions and objects are entangled—a sad scene often includes dark colors and downturned faces—so changing one risks corrupting the other. The method's soundness comes from two stages: first, the model aligns semantic understanding of the target emotion before and after editing to ensure the emotional shift is coherent; second, it explicitly preserves content unrelated to emotion so that only the emotional tone shifts. By decomposing the editing task into emotion-sensitive and emotion-agnostic components, the approach ensures emotional transformation does not accidentally alter the image's actual content or context.

Recommendation on sparse bipartite graphs fails because most user-item pairs are unobserved and the observed edges alone do not reveal latent user intents. The core insight is that intent nodes acting as intermediaries can infer what desires bridge users and items: if many users click items with shared properties, an intent node can represent that shared desire. By constructing an intent layer that enriches structural connectivity, the model creates new paths between users and items that reflect behavioral patterns rather than direct observation. Contrastive learning then enforces consistency: users with similar behavior gravitate toward similar intents, and items fitting an intent cluster together. This consistency is mathematically sound because it uses observed behavior to sculpt the intent layer, then uses that layer to predict unseen interactions by finding intents shared across users.

Conversational search fails when context contains noise and results lack interpretability. The core soundness comes from two mechanisms: logical denoising removes contradictory and irrelevant statements from context, ensuring the model receives a clean signal of user intent; generative retrieval then produces explicit, verifiable results that users can validate. Curriculum learning gradually tightens logical constraints so the model learns to handle noisy input robustly. Group relative policy optimization lets the model compare its own outputs against baselines to improve reliability. Together, these ensure the search process is both stable under messy conversation and transparent in its reasoning, so users trust the results.

Traditional web interfaces rely on fixed navigation menus that force users to hunt through hierarchies even when they know their goal. The core insight is that large language models can map user intentions to application functions if those functions are described semantically with typed inputs and outputs. By making GUI components machine-readable, Mirage allows a model to select the right tools for a stated goal and compose them into a simplified interface on the fly. This is sound because the model's language understanding can match natural-language goals to semantic component descriptions reliably, and rendering only relevant components reduces cognitive load compared to full menus. The method transfers power from designers (who build menus) to users (who speak goals), enabling personalized interfaces without redesign.
